sections.overview: The blue whale is a baleen-bearing rorqual that captures prey with an expandable throat. It occurs in every ocean except the Arctic, but its movements and population structure vary by region. Song, sightings and genetic data distinguish several population units across this wide range.
sections.identification: Its long, tapered body is mottled blue-grey, with a broad U-shaped head and a small dorsal fin far back. Each whale’s stable mottling can help identify it in photographs. Antarctic whales can reach about 33.5 metres and around 150 tonnes; northern whales about 27 metres, with females generally larger than males. About 60–88 pleats run beneath the jaw to the navel, expanding the throat during feeding. Dark, fringed baleen plates hang from the upper jaw and retain krill while water is pushed out.
sections.habitat: Blue whales follow krill concentrations, often in productive high-latitude waters during the warm season. Many move toward lower latitudes in winter, but the pattern varies: some Antarctic whales remain south and a northern Indian Ocean population is considered resident, though its movements are poorly known. Eastern North Pacific whales commonly feed off western North America and winter near Mexico and Central America; calves are seen in the Gulf of California. Antarctic, Indian Ocean and Pacific groups are distinguished by sightings, acoustics and genetics, but some regions remain under-sampled.
sections.diet: Krill, especially euphausiid crustaceans, supplies nearly all blue whale food, with prey species varying by region. At a dense patch, a whale accelerates, opens its jaws and engulfs prey and water; its throat pleats stretch around the expanded pouch. It then closes its mouth and presses water through the baleen with its tongue; krill remain caught on the fringed plates and are swallowed. This lunge-and-filter method is costly, but tag-based models show that energy gained per lunge rises sharply with krill density. Dense prey patches help build fat reserves used to fuel migration and reproduction.
sections.behavior: Blue whales are usually alone or in pairs; large feeding aggregations are rare. Their low-frequency calls include long tonal notes and repeated songs; researchers have described nine regional song types, several stable for more than 30 years. In a Northeast Pacific study combining tags and acoustic records, foraging whales sang mainly at night, while the population-level transition to migration brought more daytime song. This diel shift is a useful acoustic indicator of migration in that population; whether distant songs guide individual departures remains a hypothesis.
sections.reproduction: Females usually bear one calf, with pregnancy estimated at 10–12 months and births about every two to three years. Northern births occur mainly in winter; calves are also regularly seen in the Gulf of California. Newborns are several metres long and nurse on their mother’s rich milk for about six to eight months, sometimes while travelling toward feeding areas. Females provide the known parental care, and sparse observations mean reproductive timings remain estimates that can vary among populations.
sections.ecology: Blue whales are low-level predators that consume abundant krill and may themselves be prey for killer whales. In a laboratory experiment, faeces from pygmy blue whales stimulated photosynthesis and growth in tested phytoplankton species. This evidence comes from one subspecies under experimental conditions and does not quantify effects in the open ocean or across all populations.
sections.conservation: Mechanized harpoons and factory ships made blue whales targets of industrial whaling in the early twentieth century. The IWC records 37,000 whales killed in Antarctica in 1931, most of them blue whales; a global commercial-whaling moratorium began in 1986. For Antarctic blue whales, the IWC’s 2024 estimate is about 4,000 animals (range 1,870–8,400), or 1.9% (range 0.7–4.8%) of estimated pre-whaling abundance. Numbers have risen since the last recorded catches in 1973, yet this estimate shows continued severe depletion. The 2018 IUCN global assessment lists the species as Endangered. The IUCN’s November 2018 update lists the Antarctic subspecies as Critically Endangered. Current pressures include ship strikes, fishing-gear entanglement, underwater noise and climate-related changes to krill habitat.
